answers.stem_only: Put the code in an AWS Lambda function, create a target group of type lambda on the existing ALB, and add a path-based listener rule /convert that forwards to it; the other rules stay as they are.

Move the instances into private subnets without public IP addresses (still registered in the target group), and let the instance security group allow port 80 only from the ALB's security group instead of 0.0.0.0/0.
Set the Auto Scaling group health check type to ELB so that the group replaces instances that fail the target group health check, not only the EC2 status checks.
Consolidate onto one ALB: one HTTPS listener on 443 with all six ACM certificates (SNI), host-header rules forwarding to six target groups, and point each domain's DNS at the shared ALB.

Enable a second Availability Zone on the NLB (add a subnet in AZ B so it has a node there) and run instances in AZ B too, for example an Auto Scaling group across both zones registered with the target group.
Add one HTTPS listener on port 443 to the existing ALB, attach all three ACM certificates to it (SNI chooses the right one by host name), and keep the host-based rules.

Point the target group health check at a dedicated health path (for example /health) that returns 200 when the app is working, or widen the success codes to include 302; do not change the user-facing redirect.

Gateway Load Balancer with the appliance fleet as targets in the central security VPC, Gateway Load Balancer endpoints (PrivateLink) in each spoke VPC, and route tables that send traffic through the endpoints.
One internet-facing Application Load Balancer across the AZs with a path-based listener rule sending /api/* to a second target group and the default action to the main target group.

Put a Network Load Balancer with an Elastic IP per subnet in front of the existing ALB using an ALB-type target group; the ALB keeps its path rules and the customer allow-lists the NLB's static IPs (Global Accelerator would be the alternative).

Internet-facing ALB in public subnets for the web tier, an internal ALB in private subnets for the application tier, each tier in its own Auto Scaling group; web tier calls the internal ALB's DNS name.
NLB cross-zone load balancing is off by default; turn it on (target group or load balancer attribute) so each node spreads over all 8 targets, accepting inter-AZ data transfer charges.
Raise the target group deregistration delay (connection draining) above the longest upload, for example to 900 seconds; the Auto Scaling group waits for draining before it terminates the instance.
Imported certificates are not renewed by ACM; replace it with an ACM-issued public certificate (DNS validated) so ACM renews it automatically and the listener keeps using it.
Network Load Balancer with an Elastic IP in each subnet (static IPs) and a TCP listener forwarding to one target group of the instances; no path routing is needed, so no ALB behind it.
ALB (needed for path routing) with an HTTPS listener using an ACM certificate, forwarding to HTTPS target groups so traffic is re-encrypted from the ALB to the instances.
Quick fix without code change: enable sticky sessions (duration-based load balancer cookie) on the ALB target group.
Security groups cannot be added to an NLB created without them, so create a new NLB with a security group, allow 443 on the instances only from that security group, and move clients to the new NLB.
Add an HTTP listener on port 80 with a redirect action to HTTPS port 443 (HTTP 301).
Start an ARC zonal shift for the ALB away from the impaired Availability Zone.
TLS passthrough: Network Load Balancer with a TCP listener on 443 forwarding to a TCP target group, so the TLS session is end to end and each instance decrypts with its own certificate and key.
Externalize session state to a shared managed store, for example Amazon ElastiCache (or DynamoDB), and change the app to read and write sessions there; no stickiness needed.
